OVHcloud CLI release assets were replaced with malware

Target: OVHcloud CLI · repo
Date: 2026-10-19
Target Kind: application
Language: N/A
Cause: compromised_account_credentials
Motive: credential_theft
Transitive: true
Impact: credential_theft
Phase: distribution

Synopsis

An attacker replaced binaries on five existing OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases and changed their checksums. Customers fetching the assets during a 94-minute window received a credential stealer.

Story

A customer whose build rejected an unexpected checksum helped expose a brief replacement of OVHcloud's official command-line downloads on October 19. The software let administrators manage cloud resources, but binaries attached to five existing GitHub releases had been swapped for secret-stealing builds. The source and version tags could remain familiar while a new download supplied different executable code.

OVHcloud confirmed that a compromised developer account replaced release assets for versions 0.11.0 through 0.15.0 between 12:47 and 14:21 UTC. OpenSourceMalware reconstructed changes to the downloadable archives and their checksum files, explaining why checking a fresh download against a freshly replaced checksum list could miss the substitution. A previously pinned digest provided the customer with an independent comparison. The vendor said its source and build chain were unaffected.

The vendor's later investigation traced stolen credentials to a malicious color-picker-universal extension installed on a developer's personal MacBook a year earlier. It linked the extension's infrastructure to GlassWorm and said the stolen keys, rather than that laptop itself, were used for the release swaps. The altered CLI collected cloud configuration, SSH keys, and developer-tool data. OpenSourceMalware had independently identified earlier suspicious activity on the same GitHub account, while treating continuity of the operator as an inference.

OVHcloud removed the altered assets, released clean version 0.16.0, and enabled release immutability. It reported roughly 250 downloads during the incident, rather than 250 demonstrated executions. A build from the unchanged source was distinct from an archive obtained through the compromised release page. The bounded exposure was a download of an altered asset during the incident, not every earlier installation bearing one of the same five version numbers.
